newsitem.title: USA: US agency says cap on foreign workers not reached.
newsitem.headline: US agency says cap on foreign workers not reached.

text.p: The U.S. Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) said a re-check showed that the number of foreigners approved for entry into the U.S. to work in specialty occupations had not reached an annual limit, contrary to an earlier finding.
In August, the INS said a statistical report showed that approvals totaled 66,541, above an annual cap of 65,000. The limitation applies to the fiscal year ending September 30.
A notice from the INS on Friday said a recalculation showed that only 60,227 petitons were approved as of September 6.

The program, known as -H-1B, permits non-immigrant workers to enter the United States to perform services in occupations requiring a bacheleor's degree or higher, or as a fashion model "of distinguished merit and ability."
Occupations typically admitted under the program include architects, engineers, accountants, doctors and college professors.
The program went into effect in 1992. If confirmed, the August determination that 66,541 permits had been issued would have represented the first time the cap was reached since the program started.

The INS said it told its service centers on September 6 to resume processing almost 5,000 H-1B cases held up since August 20. The agency said it was monitoring approvals on a daily basis and did not expect the cap to be reached by the end of the month. A fresh allotment of 65,000 authorizations begins October 1.

In explaining why the earlier data were flawed, the INS said a "computer code" included all changes in previously approved employment, not just the filing of new petitions. The agency said 10,500 "duplicates" were identified, including holders of the special H-1B visa who changed jobs.

Several people in the banking industry had complained that the limitation frustated efforts to hire people to carry out risk analysis work. They said there was a shortage of qualified candidates to work on computer models used in credit decisions, or monitoring interest rate and currency risk.
The INS said it was soliciting public comment on methods to track petition approvals in the new fiscal year.

The H-1B program allows hiring of foreigners for temporary periods of up to six years. It is separate from the "green card" program under which millions of legal permanent residents receive work authorizations.
"It's very good news and we're all relieved at the recount, and that the H-1B category remains available," said Lowell Gettman, an attorney in New York specializing in immigration issues.

Still, Gettman said there was concern among employers that the U.S. Congress might reduce the cap. He said foreigners, including legal permanent residents, were targeted in other legislation, such as the welfare reform bill.

Susan Allard, head of a recruitment firm in San Francisco, said the recount was welcome news. She said if someone's H-1B expired and the cap was in place, employers could have been forced to order a worker off the premises.

But she said other problems of quotas and delays face people seeking permanent resident status. She said for some industries, U.S. productivity is being hurt by an inability to hire foreigners with the necessary skils.
Immigration is a sensitive topic in an election year, she said. "It's just such a totally hot potato that it's a bad climate to argue for increases in quotas," she said.
